title: Agency independence as statutory design and institutional practice
shortTitle: Agency independence as statutory design and institutional practice
summary: Agency independence describes limits on presidential influence created by legal structure, actual political relationships, and established practices.
notes:
For-cause removal protection, multimember leadership, staggered terms, political-balance requirements, and chair-selection rules can affect the President’s influence in different ways. The editors caution that an independent agency usually remains within the Executive Branch when it exercises powers reserved to federal officers. A label such as independent establishment may merely mean that the entity is outside a larger department.

Legal insulation and practical autonomy are separate. Presidents may gain influence through ordinary vacancies, chair designation, budgets, and informal coordination. Historical studies in the text concern particular periods and should not be generalized as current empirical findings. Agency-specific functions also matter: the materials discuss adjudication and monetary policy as settings where insulation can serve distinct purposes. Claims about optimal independence remain contested.
